questions.question: Describe the composition of the atmosphere, distinguishing permanent gases from variable components, and explain the importance of any three of them.
questions.expected_answer: By volume, dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0,93% argon and 0,04% carbon dioxide, with traces of neon, helium, methane and hydrogen. These are the permanent gases: their proportions are effectively the same everywhere in the lower atmosphere. The variable components change with place and time — water vapour from almost nothing to about 4%, dust and other aerosols, and ozone concentrated in the stratosphere. Three importances: nitrogen dilutes oxygen so combustion is controlled and supplies the raw material bacteria fix for plant proteins; carbon dioxide is the input for photosynthesis and a principal greenhouse gas despite its tiny share; water vapour supplies every cloud and every drop of rain, carries latent heat and is the most abundant greenhouse gas. Dust deserves a mention too, since each particle is a condensation nucleus on which water vapour condenses.

questions.question: Explain why temperature falls with height in the troposphere but rises with height in the stratosphere, and say what each pattern means for weather in that layer.
questions.expected_answer: The troposphere is heated from below: the surface absorbs solar radiation and re-radiates it as long-wave energy, so air nearest the ground is warmest and temperature falls with height at an average lapse rate of 6,5 °C per 1 000 metres. Warm air below cool air is unstable, so it rises, cools, condenses and produces cloud — which is why all weather occurs in this layer. The stratosphere is heated from above by the ozone layer at 20 to 30 kilometres, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation and converts it to heat, so temperature rises with height. Warm air lying above cool air is a permanent inversion: the layer is extremely stable, convection is suppressed and there is almost no water vapour, so no clouds or weather form. That stability is exactly why jet aircraft cruise in its lower reaches.

questions.question: Explain how CFCs deplete the ozone layer, describe two consequences for South Africans, and evaluate the response taken to the problem.
questions.expected_answer: CFCs were released from aerosol propellants, refrigerator and air-conditioner coolants, foams and solvents. Because they are chemically stable, rain cannot remove them and they drift slowly into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet radiation breaks them apart and frees chlorine. Chlorine destroys ozone catalytically — it is not consumed, so a single atom destroys many thousands of ozone molecules. Consequences for South Africans: more ultraviolet-B reaching a country that already receives intense sunshine, so higher rates of skin cancer, cataracts and immune suppression; and damage to phytoplankton off our coasts, which weakens the base of the marine food web that supports west-coast fisheries. The response was the Montreal Protocol of 1987, which phased out CFC production internationally; it is widely judged the most successful environmental treaty signed, because ozone concentrations are now measurably recovering. Household action still matters — old fridges and air-conditioners should be degassed by a technician rather than dumped — and personal protection with hat, shade and sunscreen remains necessary while recovery continues.
